message:
auth: set the cookie's Secure flag from the request scheme

The flag used to follow NODE_ENV, so a production build reached over plain
http://<lan-ip> set a Secure cookie the browser dropped, and login bounced
back to /login. It now follows x-forwarded-proto per request, which Next
fills from the socket when no proxy sets it. KIKOERU_SECURE_COOKIES still
forces it either way, and compose no longer defaults it to false.

extras: page the image lightbox by scroll and swipe

The lightbox now steps through every image in the work in the order the
grid shows them. Grouping by folder reorders images that interleave two
folders, so paging through the raw list jumped around.

Three ways through it: the existing arrow buttons, a wheel or trackpad
scroll on desktop, and a horizontal swipe on touch. Wheel deltas
accumulate to a threshold and a step opens a short cooldown, so a
trackpad flick's momentum tail does not fly through the gallery. The
swipe locks its axis on the first real movement, drags the image with
the finger, and eats the click that ends it so the full-bleed close
overlay does not dismiss the viewer. The two neighbouring originals are
preloaded once an image is up so moving on does not stall on a fetch.

deploy: add Docker as an optional way to run the app

A root Dockerfile, compose.yaml, .env.docker.example and .dockerignore
build a self-contained image (Node 22, production node_modules, ffmpeg)
that runs from web/ so the cwd-relative drizzle and kuromoji lookups keep
working. The library is mounted read-only at /library; data and covers
live in named volumes.

Nothing changes for node/pnpm installs. The three code changes are all
opt-in through env vars the Dockerfile or compose sets:

- KIKOERU_SECURE_COOKIES lets the login cookie work over plain HTTP.
  `next start` marks it Secure, which browsers drop on a LAN IP.
- /api/health answers without a session for the compose healthcheck.
- KIKOERU_IN_CONTAINER hides "Open folder", which has no desktop to
  hand the path to inside a container.

The README documents the Docker path, how to move an existing install
across via backup import, and that Settings -> Library paths overrides
KIKOERU_LIBRARY_ROOT once set.

search: keep the caret in the box when Escape closes the suggestions

Escape closed the suggestion list and blurred the input. Anything that
put focus back — and focus has to come back for a subsequent keystroke to
reach the box at all — fired onFocus, which reopens the list, and cmdk
highlights its first item as it mounts. Enter then took that suggestion
instead of submitting what was typed, so "Escape, then Enter to search
for exactly this" worked or not depending on whether React had flushed
the reopen before the keystroke landed.

Leave focus where it is, which is what a combobox is expected to do, and
reopen on the next keystroke instead. onFocus can no longer do that job,
since the box never lost focus to begin with.

Found because the e2e spec that covers free-text submit is written as
Escape then Enter, and it had been passing on timing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_014DWgZiktsedPGdb84M28mL

search: find works by their RJ code

Typing a work id into the search box returned nothing. The index builds a
document per work from its title, kana title and circle name; the id was
carried as refId, stored but never indexed. The only works findable by
code were the ones with no DLsite listing, because upsertWork titles
those by their own id — which is also why the e2e suite never noticed.

Works gain a `code` field holding the forms of an id that are actually in
circulation: the id itself, its bare digits for anyone who has the number
but not the prefix, and the zero-padded eight-digit form. DLsite answers
to both paddings, which is why the scanner probes both when it looks a
work up, so whichever one was copied has to find it.

A code query also turns fuzzy matching off. Ids in a library sit a digit
or two apart and at fuzzy 0.3 a ten-character term tolerates three edits,
so RJ01678210 came back with every neighbour within three digits of it
and the work asked for arrived buried among them. isWorkCodeQuery draws
the line: an rj/vj/bj prefix, or six to eight bare digits. Shorter
numbers and ordinary words keep the fuzzy matching they want.

The field is boosted above every other, since a code has to beat the type
weighting that otherwise ranks works below seiyuu, circles and tags.

The rules live in their own module, free of server-only and of the
database, so they can be tested on their own. searchSuggestions and
searchWorkIdsForQuery each carried a copy of the variant loop and the
boost table, which is how the two would have drifted apart; both now go
through rankDocs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_014DWgZiktsedPGdb84M28mL

player: keep playing when a background stall interrupts a handoff

Android reports playback pausing about a minute after an autoplay
advance, but only with the screen off, and for every format. iOS is
clean. The wav transcode shipped in the same batch and took the blame,
but it only touches .wav and serves a plain range-capable file, so it
cannot explain mp3. The two-deck handoff can.

armStandby loads the next track 30s early and leaves it paused inside a
hidden page, which is the state Chrome on Android suspends. advance()
then plays that suspended deck, downgrades it to preload="metadata", and
destroys the outgoing deck's player before the incoming one has reported
playing — a window Chrome hands to Android as "nothing is playing".
Playback runs off the prebuffered range for about a minute, then needs
the network again on a radio in power save. One error was fatal: onError
probed once, retried once, and called setIsPlaying(false). There were no
stalled or waiting listeners at all.

The trigger is the phone's power management. What made it permanent was
ours, so:

- A recovery ladder replaces the one-shot retry. waiting/stalled/playing
  are listened for, attempts back off 2/4/8/15/15s escalating from a bare
  play() to a reload and reseek, and it gives up after ~44s with a toast.
  The first rung is unhurried on purpose: waiting is also what a healthy
  deck fires while it buffers the start of a track, so nothing is
  reloaded until the clock has failed to move for six seconds.
- The outgoing deck is kept intact until its replacement fires playing,
  with a 5s fallback, so the page never owns zero live players mid-swap.
- preload is left where armStandby put it rather than downgraded at the
  moment the deck needs its buffer most.
- The prearm window drops to 10s while hidden, shortening the span in
  which a paused standby deck can be suspended. hiddenRef moves to its
  own mount-once effect so it can be trusted for that decision: the
  effect that owned it bails when the queue is empty, leaving the flag
  stuck on its last value.
- The handoff timer is re-anchored on every tick. It was fixed from a
  single timeupdate sample, so a stall left it firing into the middle of
  a track and banking that track as finished.

errorRetryRef goes with the one-shot retry it existed for.

Progress writes now check their result. They were fire-and-forget, and
the session proxy answers an unauthenticated POST with a 307 to /login
that fetch follows and reports as 200, so a lost position read as saved.
A failed write puts lastSavedRef back so the next tick retries, and
sendBeacon's return value is no longer ignored.

Not reproducible here, so this hardens every branch of the diagnosis
rather than confirming one. Two e2e specs cover it: a handoff with the
page reporting itself hidden, and a synthetic buffering hiccup that must
not restart playback.

work: let a work's play progress be cleared

Positions are written continuously while a track plays and there was no
way to take them back. A work that has been touched once keeps its
per-track bars for good and sits in the library's on-deck row for good,
because listRecentlyPlayedWorks is driven by nothing but max(updated_at)
over the work's track_progress rows.

Add a Clear progress button to the work page, in the Tracks header over
the bars it erases and only when there are some, so it is never a no-op.
It confirms first: the wipe is irreversible and can span dozens of
tracks. Likes and bookmarks are untouched.

Deleting the rows is what drops the work off on deck. Marking them
completed would not have — on deck asks only whether a row exists, not
where it sits or whether it finished — so the finished tracks go with the
part-played ones, and a test pins that.

router.refresh() alone left the bars up. Two client-side caches of a
position outlive it: the map TrackList banks on the way out of a track,
and the player's sessionPosRef, which also feeds initialPosition on a
queued track. The player gains forgetProgress(trackIds) for both, and
publishes a progressEpoch that TrackList stamps its map with, so a stale
stamp reads as empty rather than being cleared by an effect after the
fact.

Clearing while a track of the work is playing is allowed and does not
interrupt it. The player banks a position again within seconds and the
work returns to on deck, which is the honest answer for something being
played right now.

repository.test.ts is new and covers listRecentlyPlayedWorks too, which
had no test at all.

scan: let folders with no work id become works

A folder of loose audio, a Comiket release, anything bought outside
DLsite — `findWorkEntries` recursed into it, found no RJ code and dropped
it without a log line. There was no way to get it into the library.

Add an opt-in setting. A folder becomes a work when it is the shallowest
one holding audio and holding no RJ-coded work anywhere beneath it. Its
id is `LOCAL-` plus a hash of its absolute path, so discovery stays pure;
it is titled from the folder and everything else is filled in through the
existing edit dialog. Off by default: with it off neither subtree probe
runs and the scan is byte-for-byte what it was.

Nothing about such a work may be looked up, so three gates say so —
`needsMeta`, the quick-skip, and `refreshWorkMetadata` — and the
missing-seiyuu list excludes them, or its scan would force-fetch every
one. The title and `metadata_source` are insert-only, so a rescan cannot
walk back a hand-typed edit. With the setting off again these works are
filtered out of reconciliation rather than offered up for deletion.

Discovery is now one function shared with backup restore, which carried
a second copy of the same walk; a folder the scanner claimed but restore
did not is a work that silently loses its path on restore. Covers with no
parseable id fall back to the filename, which is the id.

No migration: the setting is a key in the existing `settings` table, and
`NormalizedWork["source"]` was already typed `"dlsite" | "manual"`.

Verified against the real library: 331 RJ works either way, plus exactly
the 8 expected folders, with `Images`, `Video`, `エロ` and the rest
correctly passed over.

scan: see the work ids that sit next to an underscore

`\b` treats `_` as a word character, so the trailing boundary in RJ_REGEX
refused `RJ01124146_MP3V0` — the shape DLsite's own downloader produces —
and the leading one refused `耳フェラ。_RJ191210`. 108 top-level folders in
one real library carried an id the scanner could not see, 103 of them
absent from the database entirely.

Swap both boundaries for lookaround that rejects an adjacent letter or
digit but lets `_` and punctuation through, and rejects a following digit
so 9+ digit strings still fail instead of matching their first 8.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GWNQEVyc6JU399VMgH9p8i

library: narrow the filter menu to the works still showing

The filter sheet listed every tag, voice actor and circle in the library with a
library-wide count, and that list never moved as you filtered. Picking ASMR
still offered every other tag in the collection, most of them on no remaining
work, so choosing a second one landed on an empty grid with nothing to say why.

The menu is now built from the works currently showing, with counts to match:
filter by 耳舐め and the tag list goes from 160 entries to the 136 those works
actually carry, ASMR reading 83 rather than 103. On the library this was built
against every one of those 136 leads somewhere, and the facet pass costs under
two milliseconds over 231 works.

It needs no extra query to know what matched. listWorksFiltered takes no limit
or offset and has a single caller, so the array the page already holds is the
complete filtered set and its ids are all the facets need. The lists are built
that way with or without active filters — one code path, and the counts in the
menu cannot disagree with the grid. FilterList itself is untouched: it renders
what it is handed, and maps its fuzzy-search suggestions back through the same
items, so narrowing constrains those too.

Voice actors and circles narrow the same way, which is worth being explicit
about because they are OR filters: pick one voice actor and the menu offers
only the people they have worked with, so a second, unrelated one can no longer
be added from it. The unfiltered lists therefore stay, now purely to label the
chips in ActiveFilters — a selection that has narrowed itself out of the menu
is undone from its chip, and resolving those names from the narrowed lists
would remove the way back at the exact moment it is needed.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01E2w8BpWYeKpSv8R6rT68px

library: notice when a work's folder has gone

Deleting an RJ folder left its entry in the library forever. The scanner only
ever added: it walked what was on disk and upserted, so nothing ever compared
that against what was on record, and an absence looked exactly like a work it
had not reached yet.

It now takes the set of ids it found and diffs it against the ids in the
database, stamping missing_since on the ones that are no longer there. That
drops them out of every browse surface — library, seiyuu, circles, on deck,
recently played, and the tag and voice-actor counts — while the row itself,
along with its likes, bookmarks and playback progress, stays put. Settings
lists what went missing and removes it only when you say so, because a work
that disappeared because a drive was unplugged should not take your listening
history with it.

Two guards make that safe to run unattended. Nothing is marked unless every
library root read successfully first: findWorkEntries swallows a readdir
failure and returns an empty map, so a disconnected drive is otherwise
indistinguishable from a library someone emptied. And the found-id set is
snapshotted before the incremental pass deletes the entries it decides to
skip — reading it afterwards would have flagged the entire healthy library.
Both were mutation-tested: removing either guard fails exactly the tests
written for it.

Playing a track from a folder that has gone used to leave the deck stuck on
it, retrying an element that would never load. The error handler now probes
the failing URL, and on a 404 or 410 says so and advances the queue, giving up
after three gone tracks in a row rather than walking the whole queue with a
toast for each.

scan: add an extras-only pass that never contacts DLsite

Getting extras for the first time already needs nothing but a scan: every
existing row has a null assets_scanned_at, so the next ordinary scan re-walks
each work once and then goes back to skipping it. Keeping them up to date
afterwards was the gap.

An incremental scan skips a work whose folder mtime has not moved, and that
check stats the work folder itself. Dropping a file into おまけ/ or 台本/ only
changes the immediate parent directory's timestamp, so the work folder looks
untouched and the new file stays invisible — indefinitely. The only way to
reach it was a force rescan, which finds it by re-fetching every DLsite
listing: minutes of rate-limited network to pick up a text file.

This mode re-walks every work's files and never asks DLsite for anything. On a
231-work library it reads 3236 tracks and 2410 extras in about two seconds,
where the force rescan it replaces would have made 231 network round trips.

It also covers the case where the classification rules themselves change: an
upsert plus a prune over the same walk reconciles what is recorded with what
is on disk, so a release that learns to recognise a new kind of file only
needs this to be run once.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_018rT1DnuESJNntxLhkDKLSh

work: keep the player reachable while the 台本 reader is open

Reading along with the audio is the point of having the reader, and it was
covering the one control you need while doing it. It now stops at the top of
the player bar rather than at the bottom of the viewport, and stops being modal
so what is underneath still answers to the mouse.

The bar publishes its own height, because there is no constant to hard-code:
it differs between the compact and wide layouts, moves with the safe-area
inset, and changes again when the waveform seek bar is on. Measured once on
mount as well as from a ResizeObserver — observers deliver on an animation
frame, which a background tab never gets, so a reader opened in a tab that was
never brought forward would size itself against a variable that is not there
yet. The property is cleared on unmount, so an empty queue leaves the reader
full height.

Two things had to follow from the bar being live. Outside presses no longer
dismiss, or reaching for pause would shut the reader. And the scroll keys are
claimed only for presses aimed inside the popup, since the seek and volume
sliders want the arrow keys for themselves.

That key handler moved to the capture phase: the dialog stops arrow keys from
propagating, so a bubble-phase listener on window never saw them — PageUp and
PageDown worked while the arrows silently did nothing. It finds the popup
through the DOM rather than a ref, because Base UI's Popup does not forward
one and a ref left null would have sent every key down the early return.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_018rT1DnuESJNntxLhkDKLSh

work: show the extras that ship alongside the audio

A release carries more than tracks — bonus illustrations, おまけ videos, and
台本 — and until now the scanner dropped all of it on the floor. It lands in a
pre-collapsed panel on the work page, so it is there without crowding out the
tracks.

Detection is its own pure module, because the naming is a mess in practice.
台本 is recognised from the filename or any folder above it: one release ships
eleven scripts as 台本\1　バイノーラル指示あり.txt, where only the directory
says so. Readmes are always dropped, and the Latin spellings are the minority —
リードミー and 説明書 together outnumber every variant of "readme", which
itself arrives as Read me, read_me, readme txt.txt and one Rreadme typo.
はじめに and おわりに are only readmes as a whole .txt name; as a PDF they are
illustrated booklet pages, and 【はじめに】 inside a longer name is a talk
theme.

Scripts pair with their tracks off the filename rather than tracks.track_number,
which is NULL for precisely the works this matters for — the ones named tr01_.
Both sides go through the same first-digit-run extractor, and a number claimed
by two scripts links neither, so a set split across JP/EN/CN or per character
stays unlinked instead of guessing.

A .txt 台本 reads in the app as continuous vertical Japanese. Wheel movement is
mapped onto the horizontal axis; without that a mouse does nothing at all in a
vertical-rl box. PDFs open in a new tab instead.

Gallery images are served downscaled. The originals are print resolution — 2000
x3000 and about 4 MB — so one work's twenty-two thumbnails came to roughly 90 MB
before the cache went in, which is hopeless on the phone this is mostly read
from. It mirrors lib/transcode: a capped LRU directory that is safe to delete,
falling back to the original whenever sharp cannot produce something.

Storage is one additive table plus a nullable works.assets_scanned_at, and the
column is what makes the upgrade free: every existing row has NULL there, so
the next ordinary scan re-walks each work exactly once to backfill it and then
skips it forever after. That pass reads local directories only and fetches no
metadata.

work: tap the cover to enlarge it, and transcode at 320k

Two changes, in one commit because both touch the dictionaries and the hunks
sit too close together to stage apart.

The work page's cover is now a button that opens the image full size. The
thumbnail is cropped to 4:3 by `object-cover`, so a squarer cover loses its
edges on the page; the enlarged view is `object-contain` and shows all of it,
at native resolution rather than upscaled. Escape, the backdrop and an explicit
close button all dismiss it, and focus returns to the cover.

It is not built on `DialogContent` — that is a small padded card, and undoing
its background, ring, padding and width would leave nothing of it. The portal
is reused, the popup composed alongside it with a backdrop dark enough to read
as a lightbox.

Making the cover focusable has one visible consequence: with the R18 blur on, a
click now un-blurs the thumbnail for as long as it holds focus, where before
only hover did. That follows from the existing `:focus-within` rule, and it
re-blurs as soon as focus moves. Left alone, since forcing a blur on close
would break focus restoration for keyboard users.

Transcoding moves from 192 to 320 kbps, still CBR. Constant rate is the point:
byte offset stays a linear function of time so seeking is exact, where VBR
needs the Xing TOC — 100 entries however long the file, roughly 36-second
granularity across an hour. Fine for a song, not for a two-hour work with a
waveform scrubber and bookmarks on it.

Bitrate joins the cache key, so entries from the old setting are re-converted
rather than served forever. `dropStaleSiblings` already removes any other entry
for the track, so the old files clear themselves on first replay; no manual
cache wipe.

`data/transcodes/` is added to .gitignore. The existing rules cover data/*.db
and nothing else under data/, so the cache — tens of megabytes of derived audio
per track — was staging itself.

Measured on a 61 MB mono WAV: 27.6 MB out at exactly 320000 bps, an `Info`
header with no `Xing`, duration within 27ms of the source.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01EPBdaaa2EanudWyWqvxBKR

player: send phones a compressed copy of WAV tracks

A WAV in this library runs 1.4-2.9 Mbps. A phone that drops its radio into
power-save when the screen goes off can't keep that fed, and because the
browser's media buffer is bounded in bytes rather than seconds, a high bitrate
also buys fewer seconds of slack to ride out the gap. FLAC of the same content
is half the size and doesn't stutter, which is what pointed at bitrate.

`?t=1` on the audio URL asks for a 192 kbps MP3. The server decides whether the
track's format is worth converting — lossy sources fall straight through — and
any failure (no ffmpeg, broken file, timeout) serves the original instead, so a
failed conversion can never cost playback.

The MP3 is written to a cache file and then served through the route's existing
range code, rather than piped out of ffmpeg live. That is the whole reason this
is a cache and not a stream: iOS refuses a media URL that can't answer `Range`
with a real 206 and a Content-Length, and a live pipe doesn't know its own final
length. Converting once buys a plain file every platform already knows how to
seek. Entries are keyed by source size so a re-ripped file is never served stale.

The cache is capped (KIKOERU_TRANSCODE_CACHE_MB, default 4 GB, 0 to disable) and
evicted least-recently-used, with a hit touching mtime so a track in rotation
stays hot. An entry whose work was deleted is never touched again and ages out on
its own, which is why nothing is wired into work deletion or the scanner's prune.
The entry just written is exempt from its own sweep — without that, a ceiling
below one track deletes each conversion the instant it finishes and re-runs
ffmpeg on every request.

Stored per device in localStorage alongside the other player preferences, and
defaulted from `(pointer: coarse)`: phones and tablets get the small copy, a
desktop on the same server keeps the original. Settable either way under
Settings -> Playback. `createPref` grew an optional client-side default for
this, which deliberately does not affect the server snapshot.

Measured on a 1.2 GB / 56-minute source: 28s to convert at 120x realtime, 77 MB
out, duration within 44ms of the original.

player: give phones their own now-playing layout

The seek bar ran the full width of the screen along the player's top rim,
which left nothing to aim at and no room for a thumb, and the elapsed/total
readout was desktop-only.

Below the `sm` breakpoint the player now renders a second layout: the track
and transport on one row, and the seek bar on a padded row of its own,
flanked by elapsed and total. Label widths follow the total's digit count so
the track doesn't jump at 9:59 -> 10:00. Both seek styles come along — the
line bar gains an inline variant (a 6px rounded track in a 28px touch strip
with an always-visible thumb) and the waveform is sized to 36px.

The layout is chosen from a matchMedia subscription rather than responsive
classes, so a single seek bar stays mounted — two would mean two canvases and
two resize observers painting the same waveform.

Skip back/forward are no longer hidden on phones, at 36px rather than the
desktop 32px, and the title scrolls like a ticker when it overflows: hold,
slide at a constant 40px/s, hold, ease back. The keyframe offsets follow the
distance, so a longer title takes longer to cross instead of scrolling
faster. It falls back to plain truncation when the text fits and when the OS
asks for reduced motion.

Both seek bars also clear the hover marker when a non-mouse pointer is
released — a finger never fires pointerleave, so the scrub bubble used to
stay pinned where the drag ended.

The wide layout is untouched.

player: hand off to the next track before the current one ends

Autoplay stopped advancing on Android whenever the screen was off. It
worked with the browser merely backgrounded, and it did not reproduce on
iOS.

Everything the advance needed happened after the track had already
finished: `ended` fired, React scheduled a render, the `setCurrentIndex`
updater called `loadAndPlay` from the render phase, that assigned a new
src, and only then did a cold HTTP request and a `play()` go out. Chrome
exempts a page from background throttling while it is playing audio, so
that whole chain ran in the one window where the exemption had just
lapsed and the phone was free to suspend it — and the `play()` rejection
was swallowed by a bare catch, so nothing said so.

The player now runs two alternating <audio> decks, owned by the provider
rather than the bar. Thirty seconds out, the standby deck loads and
buffers the next track; a timer armed while audio is still playing, and
therefore not throttled, hands over 0.2s before the end. The handoff is a
synchronous pause/play on an already-buffered deck: no React render, no
network, nothing left to suspend. `ended` stays on as a backstop.

Falling out of that: the side effect is gone from the state updater and
the handlers read refs instead of render-time closures; `play()`
rejections and media errors are logged and retried once; media session
metadata is set imperatively at the handoff so the lock screen is right
even when React is behind; and a hidden page stops re-rendering on every
timeupdate, pushing position state straight to the platform instead and

api: stop leaking uncaught exceptions when a stream is abandoned

Browsers abort media range requests constantly — every seek, every track
switch, every partially buffered file the player drops. `Readable.toWeb`
does not survive that: the web stream is cancelled but the Node stream
underneath keeps going, and the adapter then calls close()/enqueue() on
an already-closed controller. The resulting ERR_INVALID_STATE is thrown
from a stream callback with nobody to catch it, so every aborted request
logged an uncaughtException and left the file handle's teardown to
chance.

`lib/file-stream.ts` replaces it with an adapter that guards every
controller call and destroys the file handle on every exit — end, error,
cancel, or request abort. Used by the audio and cover routes.

Verified by hand: ten seeks and four track switches against the audio
route, previously one uncaughtException apiece, now none — with playback
still streaming continuously and no backpressure stall.

A track played to the end left its saved position sitting on its
duration. Playing it again seeked there, `ended` fired at once, and the

real duration for tracks whose length was never scanned.

`ended` now records the track as finished at position zero rather than
leaving it parked on the end, with guards so the pause/interval savers
cannot write the end position back over it, and rewinds instead of
advancing when the finished track is last in the queue.

`next build` collects page data in one worker process per core, and each
worker evaluates every route module. Connecting and migrating at module
scope meant a build against an unmigrated database had every worker racing
to apply the same migrations, failing with SQLITE_BUSY.
